claims.text: The initial material is a W–Cu composite with discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
The untreated W–Cu composite tends to develop phase separation under relevant service conditions.
The untreated W–Cu composite tends to develop interfacial voids under relevant service conditions.
The proposed intervention is addition of nanosized TiC particles during processing, with the particles dispersed along W–Cu interfaces.
Spark plasma sintering can produce the proposed uniform nanoscale TiC dispersion along W–Cu interfaces.
Moderate consolidation temperatures will promote W–Cu interfacial diffusion without causing excessive reaction.
Interfacially dispersed TiC will form a continuous, thin TiC-rich interphase between W and Cu.
The TiC-rich interphase will enhance diffusion bonding between W and Cu.
The TiC-rich interphase will reduce the thermal-expansion mismatch between W and Cu.
TiC addition will reduce the driving force for W–Cu phase separation.
TiC addition will suppress nucleation of voids at W–Cu interfaces.
A coherent TiC interlayer will facilitate phonon transport across W–Cu interfaces.
A coherent TiC interlayer will facilitate electron transport across W–Cu interfaces.
Relative to untreated W–Cu, TiC-modified W–Cu will have fewer interfacial voids and less phase separation.
Relative to untreated W–Cu, TiC-modified W–Cu will have higher effective thermal conductivity.
TiC-modified W–Cu will exhibit improved stability under high-heat-flux conditions.
TiC-modified W–Cu will exhibit improved stability under irradiation.
The intervention may cease to be effective when temperature or irradiation intensity exceeds the stability regime of the TiC interlayer.
The optimal TiC concentration and particle-size distribution have not yet been determined.

Failure of TiC-modified samples to show statistically significant improvements in both thermal conductivity and interfacial microstructure relative to a 0 wt% TiC control would falsify the proposed benefit.
